name: Where AI Falls Short
title: Where AI Falls Short
answer: Where AI Falls Short is the idea that generative AI fails in predictable ways, and knowing those failures ahead of time is most of what safe use requires. The failures do not mean a school should avoid AI, but they do mean every use needs a plan for catching mistakes. The six failures are invention, inconsistency, bias, not knowing your students, inability to be held responsible, and privacy risk from free tools that store what users type.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: The idea is that AI's limits are not random surprises but a known set of failure modes that a school can plan around. Figure 1.4 names six failures, and the text explains each one so staff can recognize it before harm reaches a student or family. The problem it solves is the false confidence that a fluent AI answer is a correct or fair one. Without a plan, an invented fact could be shared with families, an inconsistent score could be used in evaluation, or a biased detector could accuse a student of cheating. The point is not to reject AI but to treat every use as needing a human check.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the text does not divide the six failures into separate grade band routines, so the same cautions apply wherever AI is used. Anything that will be shared with families, graded, or used to make a decision needs a person to check it against a real source. A tool that cannot give the same answer twice should not be scoring a teacher's job performance, and schools should watch for bias such as essays by students learning English being flagged as machine written. Teachers should use what they know about a student, for example a boy who stopped turning in homework after his grandmother died or a girl who reads above grade level but freezes on timed tests, because AI does not know those things. When a grade is wrong or a message upsets a family, a person has to answer for it and fix it, and free tools that store what users type should not receive a student's name, disability, or discipline record.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a formal evidence label to this idea, but it cites research for some of the failures. For inconsistency, a 2026 study had eight AI systems rate 12 videos of elementary classrooms and compared the ratings with those of certified human observers, and the AI scores changed from one run to the next, matched the experts only moderately at best, and leaned on what teachers said out loud rather than what was happening in the room (Melo et al., 2026). For bias, a widely cited study found that tools built to detect AI writing often flagged essays by writers whose first language is not English as machine written when they were not (Liang et al., 2023). One test company built detectors that showed no such bias on its own adult test data, but a school cannot assume the tool it buys behaves that way (Jiang et al., 2024). The text also states that no tool on the market has eliminated invention, or hallucinations.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that invention cannot be eliminated by any tool on the market, so anything shared with families, graded, or used for a decision needs a person to check it against a real source. Inconsistency means a tool that cannot give the same answer twice should not be scoring a teacher's job performance. Bias creates the risk that a student learning English could be accused of cheating for writing simply, and AI does not know your students, so teachers' knowledge and human tutors' judgment remain necessary. Responsibility cannot sit with software, so when a grade is wrong or a message upsets a family, someone has to answer for it and fix it. Privacy is also a limit, because some free AI tools store what users type and use it to improve their products, and typing a student's name, disability, or discipline record into the wrong tool can break federal and state privacy law, which Chapter 3 covers in detail.
